explanation: Turing opens by saying the computable numbers are those whose decimal expressions are calculable by finite means, but this requires more explicit definition. He compares a person computing a number to a machine with finitely many m-configurations, a tape divided into squares, and one scanned square at a time. The machine's next action is determined by the pair of current m-configuration and scanned symbol. A computing machine prints two kinds of symbols, figures (0 and 1) and others; the subsequence of figures printed from a blank tape is the sequence computed. A machine is circular if it prints only finitely many figures, circle-free otherwise; a sequence is computable if some circle-free machine computes it, and a number is computable if it differs by an integer from a number so computed. This definition is the foundation on which the enumeration, universal machine, and undecidability results rest.

To prove no such process exists, he supposes a machine D that marks the S.D of a machine with u if circular and s if circle-free. Combining D with the universal machine I yields a machine H whose n-th section tests n and, if satisfactory, writes the R(n)-th figure of the sequence computed by M(n) as the R(n)-th figure of J'. The verdict cannot be u because H is circle-free, and cannot be s because then H would be required to compute its own R(K)-th figure, which would never be found, making H circular. Both verdicts are impossible, so no machine D exists.

explanation: Turing states that the results of §8 show the Hilbert Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution. He refers to Hilbert and Ackermann for the formulation and proposes to show there can be no general process for determining whether a given formula U of the functional calculus Z is provable. He distinguishes this from Gödel's results: Gödel showed there are propositions U such that neither U nor its negation is provable, whereas Turing shows there is no general method telling whether a given U is provable, equivalently whether Z with the negation of U adjoined is consistent. For each computing machine M he constructs a formula Un(M) whose interpretation is that 0 appears in some complete configuration of M. Lemma 1 shows that if 0 appears then Un(M) is provable; Lemma 2 shows that if Un(M) is provable then 0 appears. Hence a general provability decision process would decide whether M ever prints 0, which §8 shows impossible. Therefore the Entscheidungsproblem cannot be solved.

assumptions: The device is automatic and digital

attribution.evidence_note: The report is authored by von Neumann; the subdivision is presented in Sections 2.0-2.9.
attribution.name: John von Neumann

claim: An automatic digital computing system is analyzed into five specific parts: central arithmetic (CA), central control (CC), memory (M), input (I), and output (O), with C = CA + CC as the associative core.
conceptual_move: Replace a device-level description by a functional partition into organs defined by the role each plays in computation, storage, and contact with the outside.

curation.method: passage-grounded extraction plus separate source-grounded machine critic

explanation: Von Neumann needed a way to discuss a machine that did not yet exist without drowning in vacuum-tube circuit detail. He therefore decomposed the device by function rather than by component. The central arithmetical part CA performs the operations; the central control part CC sequences them; the memory M holds numbers, orders, tables, and intermediate results; input I and output O mediate contact with an outside recording medium R. The partition is deliberately coarse and is meant to be refined later. It also frames a key design question: which memory functions must live inside the device and which can be delegated to external media. The subdivision is not a claim about physical layout but a vocabulary for reasoning about trade-offs among speed, capacity, and complexity. It became a template for describing stored-program machines, though the report itself presents it as a preliminary orientation, not a finished architecture.

Sections on programming and input/output were never written
The partition does not by itself settle physical implementation
problem: How to describe and design a general-purpose automatic digital computing device without committing prematurely to particular hardware details.

curation.method: passage-grounded extraction plus separate source-grounded machine critic

explanation: Von Neumann lists eight distinct reasons a computing device needs memory, ranging from partial products during multiplication to boundary conditions for partial differential equations and material being sorted. These differ in purpose and in the amount of storage they demand. Rather than build separate organs for each, he argues it is tempting to treat the entire memory as one organ and to make its parts as interchangeable as possible. This move matters because it enables a single memory technology and a single addressing scheme to serve instructions, data, and tables alike. It also sets up the later capacity analysis, where the requirements of different problem classes are added or treated as alternatives. The unification is a design preference supported by the observation that existing devices already use external media for many of these functions; the question is whether a high-speed device can rely on internal memory instead.

explanation: The vacuum tube used as a gate or trigger is an all-or-none device with two equilibria; trigger circuits with more than two equilibria are disproportionately more involved. The choice is thus not merely a convention but a coupling of arithmetic representation to switching-element physics, with conversion costs pushed to the boundary.

explanation: Von Neumann explicitly postpones the electromagnetic nature of the elements. He introduces the E-element as a circle receiving excitatory and inhibitory stimuli and emitting along a branching axon after a fixed synaptic delay τ. Conduction delays along lines are neglected because at τ about a microsecond an electromagnetic impulse travels roughly 300 meters, far longer than the intended wiring. The delay is assumed dispersionless and common to all elements, and is used as an absolute unit of time to synchronize the device. This abstraction lets him draw and reason about adder, multiplier, divider, and memory networks as discrete logical structures. He stresses that the simplification is temporary: after the preliminary conclusions, the elements must be reconsidered in their true electromagnetic nature. The E-element is thus a deliberate modeling device, not a claim about neurons or about final hardware.

curation.method: passage-grounded extraction plus separate source-grounded machine critic

explanation: A single E-element that stimulates itself holds one stimulus indefinitely, giving unit memory capacity. Chaining k such elements gives k-fold capacity but costs k to 2k vacuum tubes for nothing more than a delay. Von Neumann therefore replaces the chain by a delay device dl(k) containing no E-elements, which retains a stimulus for kτ periods and re-emits it. Feeding the output back into the input converts the delay into a cyclical memory holding a stimulus indefinitely and making it available at multiples of kτ. Terminal equipment with receive, clear, and output lines turns it into a proper memory organ. This move decouples memory capacity from the number of active elements, which is essential for reaching the large capacities estimated later. The report notes that linear delay circuits can be protected against backtracking by E-elements at their ends.

assumptions: Numbers are represented with a sign digit followed by the binary point

attribution.evidence_note: Sections 9.1-9.3 develop the fixed-point convention.
attribution.name: John von Neumann

claim: Requiring the binary point to follow immediately after the sign digit confines all numbers to between −1 and 1, which guarantees that multiplication can always be carried out without overflow.
conceptual_move: Fix the binary point at a common position for all numbers so that the product of any two representable numbers is again representable.

curation.method: passage-grounded extraction plus separate source-grounded machine critic

explanation: If the binary point lies between positions i and i+1 in one factor and j and j+1 in the other, the product lies between 0 and 2^(i+j−2). To avoid special precautions against products exceeding the representable range, von Neumann requires k = i + j − 1 and then fixes i = j = k = 1, so the binary point always follows the sign digit. All non-negative numbers then lie between 0 and 1, and all numbers of either sign between −1 and 1. This makes multiplication always executable but shifts the difficulty to planning: every intermediate result must be scaled to stay in range, no addition or subtraction may produce a result outside [−1,1], and no division may have a divisor smaller in absolute value than the dividend. The report notes that violations still produce outputs, but not the intended sum, difference, or quotient, and that checking organs could signal infractions.

claim: Carrying one extra digit and rounding the 30th digit to 1 if either the 30th or 31st digit is 1 avoids the systematic bias of truncation without requiring carry propagation.

curation.method: passage-grounded extraction plus separate source-grounded machine critic

explanation: Von Neumann considers carrying multiplication and division one digit beyond the 30 digits to be kept, then omitting the extra digit. Plain truncation biases errors toward zero. The usual Gaussian decimal procedure of rounding to nearest, with ties to even, would require addition with carry digits and their inconveniences. Instead he adopts the binary equivalent of rounding ties to the nearest odd digit, suggested by J. W. Mauchly: digit pairs 00, 01, 10, 11 round to 0, 1, 1, 1. Equivalently, the 30th digit becomes 1 if either the 30th or the 31st digit was 1, otherwise 0. A rounding-off valve implements this by combining a digit with its predecessor when a second control line is stimulated. The rule is a concrete engineering compromise between statistical fairness and circuit simplicity, and it is explicitly attributed to Mauchly as a suggestion.

explanation: Binary square rooting proceeds digit by digit. For each position of the root, the partial root a formed so far is used to form 2a+1, which is subtracted from the partial remainder shifted left by two positions. If the difference is non-negative the next root digit is 1 and the difference becomes the next partial remainder; otherwise the digit is 0 and the shifted previous remainder is kept. Compared with division, the simple left shifts become double shifts, and the subtracted quantity is not fixed at the start but depends on the result obtained so far. Von Neumann notes that forming 2a+1 is particularly simple in binary, so the change involves altered connections and timing rather than substantial new equipment. explanation: Von Neumann defines the capacity unit as the ability to remember whether a stimulus was present at a given occasion, which represents one binary digit. Adding one unit for the sign and one to distinguish a number from an order gives 32 units per number. The memory is therefore subdivided into units and then into groups of 32 units called minor cycles, each holding exactly one standard number. Orders must also be formulated to occupy precisely one minor cycle. This organization simplifies synchronization and addressing: the digits of a number follow each other automatically, and the type marker in the first unit distinguishes numbers from orders. The 32-unit minor cycle is thus both a capacity accounting device and a structural unit of the code.
